summary.lead: Official summary (Congressional Research Service, Reported to House):

blocks.text: This bill excludes from gross income certain damages received by an individual due to any sexual act or sexual contact and establishes the applicable burden of proof in court proceedings regarding the characterization of such damages for federal tax purposes.

Under current law, amounts received as damages (other than punitive damages) from a judgment, award, or settlement of a claim may be excluded from gross income and, thus, are not subject to federal income tax, if attributable to a personal physical injury or physical sickness. The Internal Revenue Service (IRS) generally interprets personal physical injury to require observable bodily harm (e.g., bruising, cuts, swelling, or bleeding).

Under the bill, amounts received as damages (other than punitive damages) from a judgment, award, or settlement due to any sexual act or sexual conduct, whether or not there are medical records or observable injuries of such act or contact, may be excluded from gross income.

Further, if a judgment, award, or settlement states that damages are due to any sexual act or sexual conduct, then the IRS has the burden of proving otherwise in court proceedings related to the tax liability associated with such damages.
Finally, the bill requires the IRS to promote public awareness of the exclusion from gross income of damages related to any sexual act or sexual contact.

This bill would let people who receive money from a court judgment, award, or settlement for a sexual act or sexual contact leave that money out of their taxable income, so they would not owe federal income tax on it. Punitive damages, which are extra damages meant to punish the wrongdoer, are not covered by this exclusion.

Right now, damages can be tax-free only when they come from a physical injury or physical sickness. The Internal Revenue Service generally reads "physical injury" to mean harm you can see, such as bruises, cuts, swelling, or bleeding. The bill would remove that requirement for sexual-misconduct damages, so the money could be tax-free even if there are no medical records or visible injuries.

The bill also shifts the burden of proof in a tax dispute. If the judgment, award, or settlement says the damages are due to a sexual act or sexual conduct, the IRS would have to prove in court that the money should be taxed. In other words, the IRS would bear the burden of showing otherwise rather than the taxpayer having to prove the exclusion applies.
Finally, the bill requires the IRS to inform the public that damages related to any sexual act or sexual contact can be excluded from gross income.
